target_customer: Groups of friends who want to collect and share full resolution event photos
problem: Photos from one event are spread across many cameras and hard to pool and download at full resolution.
business_model: Free consumer photo sharing service, no monetization described

founders.name: Sam Odio
founders.background_notes: YC page describes him as 2x founder and head of product. No education or employers on the page.

founders.name: John Devor
founders.background_notes: YC page lists only the title.

exit.reason: Talent acquisition; three employees joined Facebook Photos and the service was wound down over about six weeks.

technical_complexity.rationale: Full resolution uploads, event galleries, zip downloads and native clients; standard web engineering for a small team.

defensibility.rationale: Many group photo sites existed per TechCrunch and Facebook could add the feature directly.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Facebook bought the team in April 2010 and redirected users to Facebook.

market_need_then: Group photo sharing was an established but fragmented behavior; TechCrunch noted quite a few group sharing sites already existed at launch in March 2009.

branding.domain_note: divvyshot.com now redirects to a GoDaddy for sale page.

identity.visual_style: Reviewers called it a gorgeous photo sharing site (headline of The Next Web, February 2010).

branding.community_and_virality: About 40,000 users at shutdown per PetaPixel; no merch or fan evidence found.

brand_strength.rationale: Praised design in press but a small user base and a hard to spell name; no brand driven growth found.

outcome_analysis: Divvyshot launched in private alpha in March 2009 as a group photo sharing site, reached about 40,000 users, and was bought by Facebook in April 2010 as a talent acquisition with undisclosed terms. Three employees joined Facebook Photos and the service was shut within weeks. The market was crowded and Facebook owned the underlying photo behavior, so the outcome was a soft landing for the team rather than a product exit.
notes: Funding: CB Insights shows $20K over 2 rounds and Seedtable lists a $10K seed; both are aggregator figures that conflict, so no round is recorded. Another source says it started with $10,000 in seed funding. Competitors Flickr, Picasa and SmugMug appear in a 2010 review, which is after the 2009 launch, so not listed. Founder education and prior employers not found. Echoed deal date varies (a timeline says 2010-03-02, press says 2010-04-02). Completeness pass: Round rests on a single database (Seedtable, 10K); CB Insights shows 20K over 2 rounds including the acquisition, so the figures conflict.
